title: Lesson 1: From User to Power User: What Owning Your Workflow Means
description: The line between using an AI tool and owning a workflow: what separates a user from a power user, what ownership requires, and where the payoff lives.

questions.question: A colleague's AI setup produces good results, but she cannot see how it works and must file a ticket to change anything. Which test of ownership does her setup fail?
options: Accountability, because nobody answers for the output it produces
Changeability, because she cannot open and edit the setup herself
Design, because it was built for her rather than out of her own work
Judgment, because it drafts text where a person should decide
questions.explanation: Ownership requires that you can open the setup and adjust it yourself. A flow you cannot inspect or repair is one you rent, and you lose the ability to fix it when the tool or the task shifts.

questions.question: Where does building a workflow pay off fastest?
options: On the largest or most visible task in your week
On the task a colleague most recently complained about
On the recurring task with the same shape each time
On the rarest task, because it has the most room to improve
questions.explanation: Effort pays off fastest on work that repeats on a near-fixed schedule with the same inputs and output shape, because the setup cost is repaid on every run after the first.

questions.question: What does staying accountable for an AI-drafted output actually require of you?
options: Sending it as soon as the tool reports that it is confident
Reviewing it only when the task feels unusually risky that day
Adding a disclaimer so readers know a tool wrote the draft
Checking it at the moment a wrong result still matters
questions.explanation: Accountability means a person stays in the loop at the moment the output could still be wrong, since the tool drafts but you decide what actually ships.
